introduction_markdown:
**GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD - General Certificate of Education Examination. JUNE 2025, ADVANCED LEVEL. English Language, Paper 2 (0730).**

Answer your questions either exclusively from **PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS)** or from **PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS)**.

**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - Duration: Two and a Quarter Hours.** Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION (Section A: Composition, Section B: Prescribed Texts, Section C: Creative Writing). ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you no marks.

**PART TWO (OLD SYLLABUS) - Duration: Three Hours.** Instructions to candidates: Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page. Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will earn you little or no marks. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**PART ONE (NEW SYLLABUS) - SECTION A: COMPOSITION (20 MARKS)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

figures.legende: F1: photograph (Source: Cameroon Tribune, Nov. 5, 2020) of a monkey walking alone on bare ground inside a wire-fenced enclosure; behind the fence stand a shelter with a long roof, a wooden climbing frame with a ladder and tall trees.

F2: two side-by-side photographs (Source: The North-Westerner, 3rd Edition No 003, March 2020) showing ground strewn with debris and rubble with a crowd standing near buildings in the background (left), and a collapsed wooden structure surrounded by a heap of wreckage (right), the aftermath of destruction.

Convention de numérotation (sujet à deux parties) : numero_exercice « NEW-A1 » à « NEW-A6 », « NEW-B1 » à « NEW-B4 », « NEW-C1 » et « NEW-C2 » pour la Part One ; « OLD-A1 » et « OLD-A2 », « OLD-B1 » à « OLD-B6 », « OLD-C1 » à « OLD-C4 » pour la Part Two. duree_epreuve vaut « 3h » partout (durée de la Part Two, la plus longue) ; la Part One dure 2h15 (voir introduction_markdown).

Figures F1 et F2 (photographies de presse, page 3) : reproduites sans filigrane par la méthode du skill (page propre, filtre de niveaux, recadrage) ; la qualité reste moyenne car ce sont des demi-teintes de journal. F1 est nette (un singe dans un enclos grillagé). F2 est très contrastée : on distingue des décombres, un attroupement au fond à gauche et une structure en bois effondrée à droite ; la cause de la destruction (incendie ou autre) n'est pas certaine, la légende reste donc prudente. La composition modèle s'appuie sur F1.
Sujet 'a' à 'f' de la Section A (Part One) : les compositions modèles sont des textes inventés (noms et événements fictifs) ; leur longueur (500 à 550 mots) est comptée par script.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Choose picture F1 and describe exactly what it shows (monkey, wire enclosure, shelter, climbing frame, trees).
2. A school visit to a sanctuary: the guide and the monkey.
3. The monkey's story (orphaned by hunting) and what it means.
4. The narrator's change of heart and the wildlife club.
5. Conclusion: freedom and the duty to protect it. A clear link between the picture and the composition is required.

**Model composition (535 words)**

The photograph shows a lone monkey walking across the bare, sandy ground of a wire enclosure. Behind it stand a wooden shelter with a tin roof, a climbing frame with a ladder, and tall trees whose shadows fall across the fence. Nothing else moves. The animal looks neither angry nor playful; it simply walks, as if it had followed the same path a thousand times. The picture reminded me of a visit that changed the way I look at wild animals.

Last year, our Form Five class travelled to a wildlife sanctuary for a school trip. We arrived noisy and excited, with packets of biscuits, expecting a day of fun. Our guide, a thin, soft-spoken man called Mr Fombe, led us along a dusty path to an enclosure very like the one in the picture. A monkey was walking alone near the fence. "This is Ngum," said Mr Fombe. "He has lived here for nine years."

Some of my classmates laughed and began to throw biscuits across the wire, calling the monkey to dance. Ngum did not even look up. The guide raised his hand gently, and the laughter died. "Let me tell you how he came here," he said.

Years ago, he explained, a hunter had shot a mother monkey in the forest, and her baby had been found clinging to her body. The hunter put the little one in a basket and carried him to a roadside market, where a trader offered him for sale as a pet. Fortunately, a forest officer saw the basket and brought the baby to the sanctuary. The keepers fed him with a bottle and nursed him through a fever. "He is alive today because people cared," said Mr Fombe. "But he can never go back to the forest. He never learnt from his mother how to find food or avoid danger. If we opened the gate, he would not survive a week."

I looked at Ngum again, and the picture in front of me changed. The fence, which I had taken for protection, now looked like a sad boundary between what he was and what he might have been. Behind the wire there was food and shelter, but no high branches, no companions, no river. A silence fell over the class, and nobody threw another biscuit.

On the way home, the bus was strangely quiet. I thought about the bushmeat sold in our markets, about the forests cut down for farms and timber, and about the many small monkeys that never reach a sanctuary. I realised that Ngum was not a unique case but a symbol of a larger problem.

Back at school, I spoke to our biology teacher, and together we founded a wildlife club. We invited a forest officer to speak at the assembly, painted posters on the school walls and wrote to the village chief to ask hunters to spare young animals and breeding females.

Today, whenever I see a picture of an animal behind a fence, I remember Ngum's slow walk across the sand. He taught me that freedom is not a small thing, and that human beings, who have the power to take it away, also have the duty to protect it.

**Marking grid (the paper prints the split of the 20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | A relevant treatment of the topic as set, a clear introduction, paragraphs that each develop one idea, a logical order and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied sentence structures, precise vocabulary, suitable register and tone, good use of linking words, a convincing style |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct grammar, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Writing fewer than 500 or more than 550 words, or ignoring the topic's exact wording (for example listing points instead of telling a story, or giving only one side when asked 'Do you agree?').
2. A weak plan: a long introduction, paragraphs that repeat one idea, no conclusion; or a pre-prepared composition that does not fit the question (it earns no marks).
3. Writing a composition that has no visible link with the chosen picture, or describing both pictures: the paper requires a clear connection with ONE picture.
